NCMEC acts as a clearinghouse and may forward reports to federal law enforcement. The statute also (a) provides a privacy-protection clause stating providers are not required to monitor or scan (f), and (b) prescribes civil penalties for knowing and willful failures to report. Critically, the explicit statutory text that creates the core reporting trigger (commonly subsection (a)(1) — i.e., the precise \"becomes aware\" or reporting-duty language) is not included in the provided excerpts; jurors flagged this omission. Accordingly, the consolidated view is: deploying NSP (Non-shareable policy (content should not be shared externally)) auto-flagging in the US requires geo-/jurisdiction-specific logic to (1) ensure that when auto-detection generates actual knowledge or possession of apparent CSAM the system collects and preserves the statutory data elements and initiates the reporting workflow to NCMEC (and possible forwarding to law enforcement), and (2) implement internal verification, audit logging, and retention/transfer controls to reduce false positives and limit exposure to \"knowing and willful\" failure penalties. Note: (g) restricts law enforcement disclosure of report contents and does not, in the provided text, impose a direct non-disclosure requirement on providers to users; any claim otherwise in prior reports has been corrected.
